desc: WHAT. A Dutch-owned multi-species animal breeding company supplying laying hens, turkeys, pigs, salmon and shrimp genetics worldwide. WHERE IT SITS. Breeding stock — upstream of most commercial poultry and aquaculture production. WHY IT MATTERS. Global poultry genetics is controlled by a very small number of firms, so a handful of breeding decisions propagate into billions of birds. Concentration here is tighter than in seed and attracts a fraction of the attention.

name: International Gene Synthesis Consortium
desc: WHAT. The industry body whose members voluntarily screen synthesis orders against sequences of concern and screen the customers placing them. WHERE IT SITS. The only screening regime that exists for DNA synthesis anywhere in the world. WHY IT MATTERS. It is voluntary, membership is a minority of global capacity, and no government requires any of it. **The most consequential control point in this entire industry is a trade association's code of practice.** That is a statement of fact about how the field is governed, not a prediction about anyone misusing it.

name: Benchling
desc: WHAT. The dominant cloud platform for designing and recording biological experiments, used across pharmaceutical, agricultural and academic laboratories. WHERE IT SITS. The software layer beneath the work — where constructs are designed before anything is ordered or built. WHY IT MATTERS. Design software sees the intent before the synthesis company sees the order and long before a regulator sees an application. Nothing requires it to look, and it is the earliest point at which anything about a project could be known.

name: Codex DNA / Telesis Bio
desc: WHAT. Maker of benchtop instruments that synthesise DNA and assemble constructs inside a laboratory, without ordering from an external supplier. WHERE IT SITS. The point where synthesis stops passing through a company that could screen it. WHY IT MATTERS. Order screening only works while orders are placed. A benchtop synthesiser moves the capability inside the building, and the voluntary regime above has nothing to inspect. This is the specific development that makes the screening question urgent rather than theoretical.

name: Wellcome Sanger Institute
desc: WHAT. One of the world's largest genomics institutes, sequencing at population scale and running large cellular and genetic research programmes. WHERE IT SITS. Charitably funded infrastructure that much of global genomics depends on, including reference datasets used commercially. WHY IT MATTERS. It has faced formal criticism over the use of African genomic samples in a commercial context, which the institute investigated and acknowledged. That episode is the clearest documented case of the consent question this map raises about plants arriving in human genomics, where the material came from people.

name: Nature's SAFE
desc: WHAT. A UK charity cryopreserving living cells and reproductive tissue from endangered animals, working with zoos and wildlife parks across Europe. WHERE IT SITS. The European counterpart to the American and Australian wildlife biobanks. WHY IT MATTERS. Wildlife biobanking is being built now, by charities and zoos, with no international framework governing who may later use the material or for what. The collections will outlast the consent arrangements under which they were gathered — which is exactly what happened with the older research collections.

name: Moscamed Brasil
desc: WHAT. The Brazilian facility that mass-rears insects for pest control, including production for engineered mosquito releases. WHERE IT SITS. The factory floor of open release — where the organisms are actually produced in the tens of millions. WHY IT MATTERS. Release programmes are discussed as science and are mostly logistics: rearing capacity, transport, and release schedules. Naming the production facility makes visible that this is manufacturing, at industrial volume, of organisms intended to go outside.

name: Topigs Norsvin
desc: WHAT. One of the world's largest pig breeding organisations, supplying genetics across Europe, the Americas and Asia. WHERE IT SITS. Alongside Genus/PIC at the top of global pig genetics. WHY IT MATTERS. Two companies supply a very large share of the world's commercial pig genetics. When gene editing enters breeding stock at that level, it propagates through national herds without any individual farmer making a decision about it.

name: Mowi
desc: WHAT. The world's largest producer of farmed Atlantic salmon, operating in Norway, Chile, Scotland, Canada and Ireland. WHERE IT SITS. The demand side of aquaculture genetics and feed, including engineered feed ingredients. WHY IT MATTERS. Farmed salmon spread routinely and interbreed with wild populations, and the genetics entering those populations are the product of intensive selection for farm conditions. Genetic alteration reaches wild fish without any engineered organism being involved, which is why a map of this industry cannot stop at what biosafety statutes cover.

name: Australian Frozen Zoo — threatened species cryobanking
desc: WHAT. Zoo-based cryopreservation of gametes and tissue from threatened Australian species, supporting assisted reproduction in conservation programmes. WHERE IT SITS. What decides which species a future genetic-rescue programme can even attempt. WHY IT MATTERS. Sampling choices made now, by individual institutions with no coordinating framework, set the limit of what is technically possible decades later. It is the least controversial part of this facet and quietly the most consequential.

name: KWS SAAT
desc: WHAT. A large German breeder of sugar beet, maize, cereals and oilseed rape, independent of the four majors and among the biggest seed companies in the world. WHERE IT SITS. The tier that licenses traits from the majors rather than owning them, and breeds the varieties those traits are put into. WHY IT MATTERS. Sugar beet is the crop where a single trait — herbicide tolerance — reached near-total adoption in the countries that permit it, faster than in any other crop. A breeder of this size adopting or refusing a trait effectively decides it for a whole sector.

name: DLF Seeds
desc: WHAT. The world's largest producer of forage and turf grass seed, operating across Europe, the Americas and Asia. WHERE IT SITS. Grass seed — the sector where the clearest documented spread on this map happened, in Oregon. WHY IT MATTERS. Grasses are wind-pollinated, perennial, outcrossing and often planted near wild relatives, which is the worst containment profile of any crop group. The commercial pressure to engineer them has not gone away because one release failed.

name: Groupe Florimond Desprez
desc: WHAT. A French family-owned breeder of wheat, sugar beet, potato and other field crops, operating internationally. WHERE IT SITS. The independent European breeding sector, which supplies varieties across the continent and depends on being able to use existing material freely. WHY IT MATTERS. Independent breeders are the constituency most exposed to patents on gene variants: they cannot pay licence fees at scale or retain patent attorneys, so they abandon breeding projects rather than risk infringement. The patent argument is usually framed as farmers against companies; it is also companies against companies.

name: Sakata Seed
desc: WHAT. A large Japanese vegetable and flower breeder operating worldwide, one of the handful of firms that dominate global vegetable seed. WHERE IT SITS. Vegetable seed — a market as concentrated as row crops and with almost none of the public attention. WHY IT MATTERS. Most of what is eaten fresh anywhere in the world descends from varieties bred by fewer than ten companies. That concentration reaches every kitchen and is argued about by almost nobody.

name: Bucher / agricultural machinery and data
desc: WHAT. A Swiss agricultural machinery group, part of the equipment layer that increasingly collects field-level data alongside the operation it performs. WHERE IT SITS. Between the seed and the harvest, gathering the data that digital agriculture platforms consume. WHY IT MATTERS. Machinery telemetry is where agronomic data originates. Who owns it is decided in equipment purchase contracts rather than in agricultural policy, and farmers frequently discover the terms after buying.

name: WHO — human genome editing governance framework
desc: WHAT. The World Health Organization's governance framework and recommendations on human genome editing, together with a registry of relevant research. WHERE IT SITS. The only global attempt to govern human genetic engineering, and it is advisory. WHY IT MATTERS. It recommends a registry, whistleblowing mechanisms and a prohibition on heritable editing until safety and societal questions are settled. None of it binds anybody. The one case that has happened was stopped by a national criminal court, not by this framework.

name: Beam Therapeutics
desc: WHAT. A company developing base editing, which changes a single DNA letter without cutting both strands, in clinical trials for blood disorders. WHERE IT SITS. The generation past CRISPR-Cas9, designed to avoid the double-strand break that causes the largest unintended rearrangements. WHY IT MATTERS. Each generation of tool is offered as the answer to the previous one's off-target problem. That is progress, and it is also an admission: the earlier tools had the problem while they were being used on people, and were described as precise at the time.

name: Prime Medicine
desc: WHAT. A company developing prime editing, which writes new sequence at a target site using a template carried by the guide RNA. WHERE IT SITS. The most flexible editing approach yet to reach clinical development. WHY IT MATTERS. Prime editing narrows the gap between reading a genome and rewriting it to specification. The regulatory categories in every country on this map were drawn around inserting foreign DNA, and a technique that writes new sequence without inserting a transgene sits outside most of them by construction.

name: Arcadia Biosciences
desc: WHAT. An agricultural company using non-transgenic breeding and editing for traits including reduced-gluten wheat and altered oil composition. WHERE IT SITS. Deliberately outside the transgenic category, and outside the regulatory scheme built around it. WHY IT MATTERS. A company can now design its product to fall outside the definition rather than through it. The regulatory question is answered at the design stage, before any application exists, which is not how any of these frameworks assumed products would be developed.

name: Element Biosciences
desc: WHAT. A sequencing instrument company competing directly with Illumina on price per genome. WHERE IT SITS. The first serious challenge to a near-monopoly on sequencing instruments in over a decade. WHY IT MATTERS. Instrument competition lowers the cost of reading genomes, which spreads capability wider and faster. Every argument on this map about who can do this work assumes a cost that is still falling.

name: Ultima Genomics
desc: WHAT. A sequencing company that announced a very low cost per genome on a purpose-built high-throughput instrument. WHERE IT SITS. The volume end of sequencing — built for population-scale programmes rather than single samples. WHY IT MATTERS. Cost per genome is the variable that determines whether sequencing a whole population is a research project or a routine service. Below a certain price it becomes the default, and the consent and retention questions arrive for everybody at once.

name: New England Biolabs
desc: WHAT. A major supplier of the enzymes molecular biology runs on — restriction enzymes, polymerases, ligases, and the Cas proteins used in editing. WHERE IT SITS. Further upstream than synthesis: the tools that cut, copy and join the DNA. WHY IT MATTERS. Enzyme supply is the least examined chokepoint in the whole chain. No screening regime, voluntary or otherwise, covers who may buy a Cas nuclease, and it is sold from a catalogue.

name: Tropic Biosciences
desc: WHAT. A company gene-editing tropical crops — non-browning banana, disease-resistant banana, decaffeinated coffee — for markets in producing countries. WHERE IT SITS. Editing aimed at crops grown in low-income countries and consumed in wealthy ones. WHY IT MATTERS. Banana is grown from clones, so a single variety dominates world trade and a disease that reaches it reaches everything. The editing answers a vulnerability created by the monoculture, and the monoculture is not what is being changed.

name: African Union — continental biosafety and biotechnology policy
desc: WHAT. The African Union's continental frameworks on biosafety and biotechnology, including the model law that many national statutes were drafted from. WHERE IT SITS. Above the national regulators on a continent where most frameworks were written with external technical assistance. WHY IT MATTERS. A model law spreads a regulatory approach across dozens of countries in one act of drafting, long before any product application appears. Whoever writes the model is doing more to decide outcomes than any national committee.

name: Ministry of Agriculture — GMO prohibition
desc: WHAT. Serbia's agriculture ministry, administering a law that prohibits the commercial cultivation and marketing of GM crops outright. WHERE IT SITS. One of the strictest positions in Europe, and a standing obstacle in the country's EU accession talks. WHY IT MATTERS. EU accession requires aligning with the EU framework, which permits authorised GM products. A country's prohibition therefore becomes a trade negotiation rather than a domestic decision — the same mechanism that operated on Mexico, arriving by a different route.

name: Ministry of Environment and Water — GMO register
desc: WHAT. Bulgaria's competent authority, operating under a law with some of the widest cultivation buffer distances in the EU and a prohibition on GM crops in and near protected areas. WHERE IT SITS. A national framework built on distance and place rather than on the product. WHY IT MATTERS. Buffers written into statute are enforceable in a way that coexistence guidance is not, and they concede the point that pollen travels. Most frameworks avoid conceding it by leaving the distances to guidance.

name: Sri Lanka — food labelling and import control
desc: WHAT. The health ministry administering GM food labelling requirements in a country that imports most of its processed food and grows no GM crops. WHERE IT SITS. The import-and-label position, which is what most of the world actually operates. WHY IT MATTERS. Labelling requirements in importing countries are enforced by testing at the border, which requires laboratory capacity most importing countries do not have. A rule that cannot be tested for is a rule that exists on paper, and that is the ordinary condition rather than the exception.

name: SEARCA — regional biotechnology information
desc: WHAT. The Southeast Asian regional centre for graduate study and research in agriculture, which runs biotechnology information and capacity-building programmes across the region. WHERE IT SITS. Where regional regulatory capacity and public messaging are built simultaneously, with donor funding. WHY IT MATTERS. Capacity-building and promotion arrive in the same programme, from the same funders. That is not hidden, and it means the officials assessing applications were often trained by organisations with a position on the outcome.

name: Regeneron Genetics Center
desc: WHAT. A pharmaceutical company's in-house genetics operation, which has sequenced the exomes of millions of volunteers through partnerships with health systems and biobanks. WHERE IT SITS. Where a drug company owns population-scale human genetic data outright rather than licensing access to it. WHY IT MATTERS. Participants consented to research through their health system. The resulting dataset is a corporate asset that outlasts the study, the consent form and in many cases the health system that gathered it. This is the human counterpart of the germplasm question the seed facet raises.

name: bluebird bio — the insertional oncogenesis cases
desc: WHAT. The FDA safety record covering cases in which patients treated with lentiviral gene therapy later developed blood cancers, prompting trial holds and investigations. WHERE IT SITS. The known and long-predicted risk of inserting genetic material into a genome: it can land somewhere that matters. WHY IT MATTERS. Insertional oncogenesis was the reason gene therapy stalled in the 2000s, and it recurred with newer vectors. The field's answer is better vectors, which is the same answer given last time. The risk is not hidden — it is disclosed, monitored and accepted, and patients carry it.

name: Moderna
desc: WHAT. A messenger RNA company producing vaccines and, increasingly, individualised cancer therapies built to a patient's own tumour sequence. WHERE IT SITS. Genetic medicine manufactured per patient rather than per product. WHY IT MATTERS. A therapy designed for one person cannot be trialled the way a product is. Regulators are being asked to approve a manufacturing process rather than a medicine, which is a different question from the one every framework on this map was built to answer.

name: Institute for Clinical and Economic Review
desc: WHAT. An independent body that assesses whether a drug's price is justified by the benefit it delivers, publishing value-based price benchmarks including for gene therapies. WHERE IT SITS. Between a company's launch price and what a health system agrees to pay, with no legal power over either. WHY IT MATTERS. Its benchmarks for several gene therapies have come in well below the launch price, and the therapies launched at the higher figure anyway. It is the clearest available demonstration that pricing in this facet is set by what a market will bear rather than by any assessment of worth.

name: a16z Bio + Health
desc: WHAT. The life-sciences arm of a large venture firm, funding synthetic biology, computational biology and health technology companies from formation onward. WHERE IT SITS. Among the funds that decide which biological problems get worked on at all. WHY IT MATTERS. Venture theses are published. Reading what a fund says it is looking for tells you which products will exist in five years more reliably than any regulator's pipeline, because the fund's statement precedes the company that will file the application.

name: NIH RePORTER
desc: WHAT. The searchable database of every grant the US National Institutes of Health has funded, with amounts, investigators, institutions and resulting publications. WHERE IT SITS. The largest single source of public money in biomedical research, published in full. WHY IT MATTERS. It answers the question the industry's own materials avoid: how much of this was paid for publicly. A grant record showing public funds, a university and a commercial partner on one project is the documented start of nearly every licence this map complains about.

name: BARDA — Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority
desc: WHAT. The US agency funding late-stage development of vaccines, therapeutics and platform manufacturing, including engineered biological products. WHERE IT SITS. Between public money and private manufacturing capacity, in the space between health policy and security policy. WHY IT MATTERS. Public funding of manufacturing capacity produces privately owned plants. When the capacity is needed, the terms on which the public can use what it paid for are whatever the original contract said, and those contracts are rarely read at the time they are signed.

name: Alliance for Science / Cornell — agricultural biotechnology communications
desc: WHAT. A communications and training programme, originally funded by the Gates Foundation and hosted at Cornell, running advocacy and fellowship programmes for agricultural biotechnology worldwide. WHERE IT SITS. Where philanthropic money funds public argument rather than research. WHY IT MATTERS. It trains fellows from countries where approval decisions are pending, which is legitimate advocacy and is also an input into those decisions. Listed at low trust: it is a voice, not a record, and the trust filters exclude it accordingly.

name: Zoetis
desc: WHAT. The world's largest animal health company, selling vaccines, diagnostics and medicines for livestock and companion animals, spun out of Pfizer. WHERE IT SITS. The health side of industrial animal production, including recombinant vaccines and genomic testing services for breeders. WHY IT MATTERS. Animal health at this scale exists because of how animals are kept. The products manage the disease pressure that confinement creates, which makes the company both a beneficiary of intensive production and one of the reasons it remains viable.

name: Neogen
desc: WHAT. A supplier of food safety diagnostics and animal genomics services, including the tests used to detect GM content in grain and food. WHERE IT SITS. The testing layer — what an importer, certifier or regulator uses to find out what is in a shipment. WHY IT MATTERS. Detection depends on knowing what to look for. Event-specific tests exist for approved transgenic events; for gene-edited organisms with no inserted sequence there is generally nothing to target. The instruments work, the reference material does not exist, and that follows from deregulation rather than from chemistry.

name: Revive & Restore — black-footed ferret cloning
desc: WHAT. The programme that produced cloned black-footed ferrets from cell lines banked in the 1980s, introducing genetic variation absent from the living population. WHERE IT SITS. The first cloning of an endangered native species in the United States, and the clearest working case of genetic rescue. WHY IT MATTERS. It worked, and it depended entirely on tissue banked decades earlier by people who had no idea what it would be used for. Whatever else this map argues, the case for cryobanking is made here — and so is the case that sampling choices made now decide what is possible later.

name: Oxitec — US releases and EPA experimental use permits
desc: WHAT. The EPA record of experimental use permits for releases of engineered Aedes aegypti in Florida and California. WHERE IT SITS. Engineered insects released in the United States, permitted under pesticide law rather than under a biosafety statute. WHY IT MATTERS. The organism is regulated because it acts as a pesticide, so the assessment asks pesticide questions. The Florida releases went ahead over documented local objection, and the permitting route meant the objection had to be made in a pesticide docket most residents did not know existed.

name: CRISPR Therapeutics
desc: WHAT. The company co-founded by Emmanuelle Charpentier, partnered with Vertex on the first approved CRISPR therapy and running its own programmes in cancer and diabetes. WHERE IT SITS. The commercial vehicle attached to one side of the foundational patent dispute. WHY IT MATTERS. Every foundational CRISPR scientist has a company. That is neither hidden nor unusual in this field, and it means the people best placed to explain the technology's limits are also the people whose companies depend on it being adopted.

name: Temasek — agri-food and life sciences
desc: WHAT. Singapore's state investment company, a substantial investor across agricultural technology, alternative protein and life sciences worldwide. WHERE IT SITS. Sovereign capital with a stated food-security rationale, investing in the technology of a sector its own country barely has. WHY IT MATTERS. An import-dependent state investing in the production technology it depends on is a rational strategy and a novel form of ownership: the investor is a government, the assets are elsewhere, and the people affected are in neither place.

name: Fonterra
desc: WHAT. The world's largest dairy exporter, a New Zealand farmer-owned cooperative supplying dairy ingredients to markets worldwide. WHERE IT SITS. A buyer whose market-access requirements set what its supplying farmers may do. WHY IT MATTERS. New Zealand's dairy brand depends on a pasture-fed image, which makes GM feed a commercial question before it is an environmental one. A cooperative of this size deciding against a trait removes the market for it across an entire national sector, without any regulator involved.

name: Guangzhou Wolbaki — mosquito production
desc: WHAT. A Chinese company mass-rearing Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes for release, operating what has been described as one of the largest mosquito factories in the world. WHERE IT SITS. Production capacity for open release at industrial scale, outside the Western programmes usually discussed. WHY IT MATTERS. Release programmes are limited by rearing capacity, and capacity is being built where labour and land are cheapest. A map of open release that only covers Oxitec and the World Mosquito Program is missing where the insects are actually produced.

name: African Centre for Biodiversity — corporate research
desc: WHAT. The continent's leading independent research organisation on seed, biosafety and agricultural corporate power, publishing country-level analysis and company profiles. WHERE IT SITS. Almost the only independent capacity on this subject in Africa, where most analysis is produced by parties with a position. WHY IT MATTERS. Its work is the counterweight to industry-funded information centres in the same countries, and it is a fraction of their size and budget. That asymmetry decides what most people in those countries read about this subject.

name: Grain SA and the commercial maize sector
desc: WHAT. South Africa's commercial grain producers' organisation, representing farmers in a country where GM maize is a staple food rather than animal feed. WHERE IT SITS. The farmer constituency inside the only African country growing engineered staples at scale for two decades. WHY IT MATTERS. South African farmers have two decades of direct experience of these traits, including resistance failures that required withdrawing and replacing stacked events. Their record is the longest continuous account of what happens on the ground outside the Americas.

name: INASE — seed royalties and farm-saved seed
desc: WHAT. Argentina's seed institute, running variety registration and the enforcement of breeders' rights against unauthorised seed trade. WHERE IT SITS. The centre of a decades-long dispute over whether a farmer may replant their own harvest. WHY IT MATTERS. Argentina grows engineered soy at enormous scale on a seed law that permits farm-saved seed, so the companies collect through private contracts and testing at delivery points instead. When a law does not give a company what it wants, the contract does — and the contract is not public.

name: Federation of Seed Industry of India
desc: WHAT. The industry body representing private seed companies in India, active on trait fees, price controls and the regulatory treatment of gene editing. WHERE IT SITS. The commercial voice in a market where the government caps seed prices and trait fees by order. WHY IT MATTERS. India is the one large market where the state sets what a trait may be charged for. The resulting dispute is the clearest test anywhere of what happens when a government treats a patented trait as a utility rather than a product.

name: CONAHCYT — native maize and public research
desc: WHAT. Mexico's national science council, which funds research on native maize diversity and produced much of the evidence behind the country's constitutional prohibition. WHERE IT SITS. Public science supporting a national restriction rather than an approval. WHY IT MATTERS. It is the clearest case on this map of a state research body producing the evidence that a government then used to restrict an industry. Everywhere else the equivalent institutions are producing the evidence used to permit one.

name: IUCN — synthetic biology and biodiversity conservation
desc: WHAT. The IUCN's process on synthetic biology in conservation, including its assessment of engineered organisms used for conservation purposes and the members' motions on gene drives. WHERE IT SITS. Where the world's conservation bodies decide, collectively, whether to become users of this technology. WHY IT MATTERS. IUCN membership includes states, agencies and most large conservation organisations, so its position shapes what is fundable and permissible across the sector. It has repeatedly declined to endorse a moratorium and equally declined to endorse deployment, which leaves the question open in the one forum equipped to close it.

name: American Chestnut Research and Restoration Project — SUNY ESF
desc: WHAT. The university programme that developed the blight-resistant Darling chestnut and filed for deregulation, publishing its data and its setbacks. WHERE IT SITS. A public university seeking permission to release an engineered tree permanently into wild forest. WHY IT MATTERS. The programme published performance problems with its own line and the sponsoring conservation organisation withdrew support as a result. Self-reported adverse findings from a developer are rare enough on this map to be worth marking wherever they occur.

name: Colossal Foundation
desc: WHAT. The non-profit arm of Colossal Biosciences, funding conservation projects and biobanking alongside the company's commercial de-extinction work. WHERE IT SITS. Between a venture-funded company and the conservation sector whose credibility it needs. WHY IT MATTERS. A company foundation funding conservation partners creates relationships with the organisations best placed to object. That is ordinary corporate practice and it is worth naming when the sector concerned is the one asked to evaluate the company's core claim.

name: Frozen Ark Project
desc: WHAT. A UK-based consortium of zoos, museums and universities banking DNA and viable cells from endangered animals, coordinating collections across institutions. WHERE IT SITS. The nearest thing to a coordinating framework in wildlife biobanking, which otherwise happens institution by institution. WHY IT MATTERS. Coordination decides whether banked material is findable later. A sample nobody can locate is the same as no sample, and most wildlife biobanking is currently accumulating in freezers with no shared index.

name: Target Malaria — Imperial College programme record
desc: WHAT. The academic side of the gene-drive mosquito programme, publishing the modelling, containment protocols and the phased pathway toward a drive release. WHERE IT SITS. The research base behind the furthest-advanced gene-drive programme in the world. WHY IT MATTERS. The published pathway is explicit that a drive release is intended, in a malaria-endemic African country, and the modelling of cross-border spread is in the literature. Nobody has to speculate about intent here; it is stated, and the governance question is what has not been answered.

name: Cibus
desc: WHAT. A company using non-transgenic editing to develop crop traits including disease resistance and herbicide tolerance, licensing them to seed companies. WHERE IT SITS. The trait-development tier working entirely outside the transgenic category, and the first company whose canola was ruled non-GM in several jurisdictions. WHY IT MATTERS. Its Canadian canola is the entry in the CFIA register with no OECD identifier, which is the concrete case behind the abstract point: a commercial product in the field that the international tracking system cannot name.

name: Bayer — Crop Science product safety summaries
desc: WHAT. The company's published safety and stewardship material for its crop products, including the resistance-management requirements attached to its traits. WHERE IT SITS. The stewardship layer — what a company asks its customers to do to keep a trait working. WHY IT MATTERS. Refuge requirements and rotation guidance are conditions of sale, enforced commercially rather than legally in most places. Compliance is measured by the company selling the trait, and where it has been measured independently it has been found lower than reported.

name: Center for Food Safety — animal biotechnology litigation
desc: WHAT. The organisation that brought the litigation over the approval of engineered salmon, and which publishes its filings and the agency records obtained through them. WHERE IT SITS. The one sustained legal challenge to engineered animal approvals in the United States. WHY IT MATTERS. A court found the agency had not adequately assessed the environmental consequences of spread, which is a procedural finding rather than a safety one — and procedural findings are what courts actually deliver in this field. The filings are a working template for anyone attempting the same elsewhere.

name: Genus — PRRS pig commercialisation record
desc: WHAT. The company's disclosures on the regulatory approvals and market entry pathway for its gene-edited PRRS-resistant pig across the US, Japan, Mexico, Brazil and Canada. WHERE IT SITS. The first gene-edited food animal moving through multiple national approvals at once. WHY IT MATTERS. Approvals are being sought in sequence across jurisdictions, and each one makes the next easier to argue for. Watching a single product move through five regulators is the clearest available view of how a precedent is actually built.

name: Novartis — Zolgensma outcomes-based agreements
desc: WHAT. The company's disclosures on instalment and outcomes-based payment arrangements for its multi-million-dollar gene therapy with health systems and insurers. WHERE IT SITS. The financial engineering that makes a one-time multi-million-dollar therapy purchasable at all. WHY IT MATTERS. Paying over years, or paying only if the therapy works, is how the price is made to fit a budget rather than how it is reduced. The arrangements are commercially confidential, so the actual price paid by any health system is generally not public.

name: Alliance for Regenerative Medicine — sector data
desc: WHAT. The trade association's published counts of trials, financings and approvals across cell and gene therapy, quoted widely including by critics. WHERE IT SITS. The standard source for how big this facet is, produced by the facet. WHY IT MATTERS. Useful data from an interested party is the ordinary condition of information in this field rather than an exception. Cite it and say whose it is; the numbers are as good as anything independent, and there is nothing independent.

name: Thermo Fisher — Patheon and clinical services
desc: WHAT. The contract development, manufacturing and clinical trial services arm of Thermo Fisher, covering formulation, manufacture and trial logistics. WHERE IT SITS. The same conglomerate that supplies the reagents and instruments also runs the manufacturing and the trial supply chain. WHY IT MATTERS. Vertical integration across reagents, instruments, manufacturing and trial services gives one company a view of the field no regulator has, and gives its customers a dependency they cannot easily unwind. Neither is unlawful; both are structural facts nobody is examining.

name: Advarra
desc: WHAT. The largest commercial institutional review board in the United States, providing ethics review for clinical trials as a paid service to sponsors. WHERE IT SITS. Where the ethics approval for a trial is bought from a vendor by the party running the trial. WHY IT MATTERS. Commercial IRBs are legal, accredited and efficient, and they are selected and paid by the sponsor whose protocol they review. The structural conflict is identical to the one in safety studies, and it applies to the body whose entire function is to protect participants.

name: AquaChile / Agrosuper
desc: WHAT. Chile's largest salmon producer, part of a group that is also among the country's biggest pork and poultry operations. WHERE IT SITS. The second-largest farmed salmon industry in the world, in a country with no native salmon. WHY IT MATTERS. Atlantic salmon in Chile are an introduced species farmed at enormous scale, and spread have established feral populations in Patagonian rivers. The genetics involved are selected rather than engineered, which is exactly why this belongs on the map: the spread and establishment happened without anything a biosafety framework would have looked at.

name: Norwegian Institute of Marine Research — spread monitoring
desc: WHAT. The state institute that monitors farmed salmon spread and the genetic introgression of farmed fish into wild Norwegian rivers, publishing annual assessments by river. WHERE IT SITS. The only systematic long-term monitoring of genetic introgression from farmed animals into wild populations anywhere in the world. WHY IT MATTERS. It has documented farmed genetics in a large majority of assessed wild salmon populations. That is a measured, river-by-river record of exactly the process this map argues about for crops — and it exists because one country decided to fund the monitoring.

name: MHRA — Innovative Licensing and Access Pathway
desc: WHAT. The UK regulator's accelerated route for medicines including advanced therapies, offering earlier engagement and a faster path to market. WHERE IT SITS. National competition for where advanced therapy companies choose to seek approval first. WHY IT MATTERS. Regulators now compete to be chosen. That is stated policy rather than an accusation, and it exerts a steady downward pressure on how demanding any one of them can be without losing the applications to another.

name: Syncona
desc: WHAT. A listed UK investment company that founds and funds life-sciences businesses, holding them for long periods rather than seeking rapid exits. WHERE IT SITS. Patient capital in a sector where the fund lifetime usually sets the pace. WHY IT MATTERS. It is the counter-example to the venture-timeline argument this map makes elsewhere, and worth holding: a longer horizon changes what gets built, and the model exists and is publicly listed. Whether it produces different products is testable rather than assumed.

name: BGI — MGI Tech instruments
desc: WHAT. The instrument arm of the BGI group, manufacturing sequencers sold internationally in competition with Illumina. WHERE IT SITS. Non-Western sequencing hardware, subject to export controls and procurement restrictions in several countries. WHY IT MATTERS. Sequencing capacity is now a subject of trade and security policy rather than only of science policy. Which instruments a country's laboratories may buy is decided by governments, and that decides what genomics that country can do.

name: European Investment Bank — life sciences lending
desc: WHAT. The EU's lending institution, providing venture debt and growth financing to European biotechnology and agricultural technology companies. WHERE IT SITS. Public money lent rather than granted, on terms set by a bank rather than by a research council. WHY IT MATTERS. Lending carries no publication requirement and no accountability to a legislature over what is produced, unlike a research grant. Public capital reaches this industry through a channel with none of the disclosure the grant channel has.

name: Enza Zaden
desc: WHAT. A large family-owned Dutch vegetable breeder operating in more than twenty-five countries, with substantial resistance-breeding programmes. WHERE IT SITS. The Dutch vegetable-breeding cluster, which supplies a very large share of the world's vegetable seed from one small region. WHY IT MATTERS. A handful of firms in one province breed most of what the world eats fresh. That geographic concentration is a single-point vulnerability nobody treats as one, and it is invisible from any national statistic.

name: Bejo Zaden
desc: WHAT. A Dutch vegetable breeder with a substantial organic seed programme alongside its conventional lines. WHERE IT SITS. The same cluster, and one of the few large breeders producing certified organic seed at scale. WHY IT MATTERS. Organic growers depend on organic seed, and very few large breeders produce it. If the organic seed supply narrows, organic certification becomes harder to maintain regardless of how the growing is done — which makes seed supply a quiet lever on the whole sector.

name: Beck's Hybrids
desc: WHAT. The largest family-owned retail seed company in the United States, licensing traits from the majors and selling directly to farmers. WHERE IT SITS. The retail tier — where a farmer actually buys, and where the trait fee is collected. WHY IT MATTERS. Independent retailers license the same traits as everyone else, so the visible competition at the point of sale sits on top of a trait layer with almost none. What looks like a choice of companies is a choice of bags.

name: Corteva — seed applied technologies
desc: WHAT. The coatings, treatments and biologicals applied to seed before sale, including neonicotinoid insecticides and microbial products. WHERE IT SITS. Between the seed and the soil — a layer of chemistry and living organisms that travels with every bag. WHY IT MATTERS. Treated seed is often outside pesticide-use reporting because nothing is sprayed, so the area treated is not recorded anywhere. It is one of the largest applications of insecticide in world agriculture and among the least documented.

name: Verve Therapeutics
desc: WHAT. A company developing single-dose base-editing therapies intended to permanently lower cholesterol, in early clinical trials. WHERE IT SITS. The first serious attempt to use permanent genome editing for a common chronic condition rather than a rare fatal one. WHY IT MATTERS. Every argument for accepting an irreversible edit rests on the alternative being worse. Applied to a condition already managed by daily tablets, that argument has to be made differently, and the size of the eligible population is orders of magnitude larger.

name: Mammoth Biosciences
desc: WHAT. A company co-founded by Jennifer Doudna developing compact CRISPR proteins for therapeutics and diagnostics. WHERE IT SITS. The search for smaller editors that fit inside the viral vectors used to deliver them. WHY IT MATTERS. Delivery, not editing, is the constraint on genetic medicine. Whoever solves getting an editor into the right tissue at scale determines what becomes treatable, and that is an engineering race rather than a biological discovery.

name: Colossal — Breaking spin-out and IP licensing
desc: WHAT. The company's own account of the technologies it develops and spins out, including plastic-degrading enzymes and computational tools. WHERE IT SITS. Where a de-extinction venture converts its research into sellable assets unrelated to any animal. WHY IT MATTERS. It is the clearest available statement of what these ventures are monetising. Read alongside the mammoth publicity, it shows the business is the platform and the spin-outs, and the animal is the reason anyone funds them.

name: Alpha Genesis
desc: WHAT. A commercial primate breeding and research facility in South Carolina, one of the largest private colonies in the United States. WHERE IT SITS. The private end of primate supply, alongside the federally funded national centres. WHY IT MATTERS. Spread from primate facilities have happened and been reported publicly. Containment failures in this facet involve intelligent social animals in populated areas, and the incidents are documented by local news rather than by any register.

name: Ace Animals / laboratory dog and cat supply
desc: WHAT. The USDA animal welfare inspection reports, which cover licensed dealers and research facilities and record every citation. WHERE IT SITS. The enforcement record for the parts of the animal trade the Animal Welfare Act does reach. WHY IT MATTERS. Inspection reports are public, searchable and specific, naming the facility and the violation. For dogs, cats and primates this is the most detailed public accountability record in this facet anywhere in the world — and it still excludes the rodents that are the overwhelming majority.

name: Fairfax Cryobank / California Cryobank — donor limits
desc: WHAT. One of the largest US sperm banks, publishing family-limit policies that cap how many families may use one donor. WHERE IT SITS. Where the only limit on a donor's offspring is a private company's policy. WHY IT MATTERS. The limits are voluntary, self-enforced, and count families rather than children. Nothing counts across banks or across borders, and donor-conceived people have repeatedly found sibling groups far larger than any published cap implies.

name: Donor Sibling Registry
desc: WHAT. A registry through which donor-conceived people, parents and donors find one another, run independently of the clinics and banks. WHERE IT SITS. The only mechanism connecting people the industry's own records keep apart. WHY IT MATTERS. It exists because the clinics did not build it. The sibling groups it has surfaced are the primary public evidence that family limits are not working, and that evidence was assembled by the people affected rather than by any regulator.

name: Indian Council of Medical Research — ART regulation
desc: WHAT. India's medical research council, whose guidelines underpin the Assisted Reproductive Technology Act and the surrogacy legislation that followed it. WHERE IT SITS. The regulator of a sector that was, before the law, the world's largest commercial surrogacy market. WHY IT MATTERS. India prohibited commercial surrogacy for foreign clients and then for almost everyone. The market did not stop; it moved to other countries with weaker rules. **A national prohibition on a cross-border service relocates it rather than ending it**, and the people most exposed move with it.

name: UPOV — International Union for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants
desc: WHAT. The intergovernmental organisation administering the plant variety protection treaty, whose 1991 act narrows what farmers may do with saved seed. WHERE IT SITS. Underneath the seed laws of most countries on this map, because accession to UPOV 1991 is routinely required by trade and aid agreements. WHY IT MATTERS. UPOV 1991 is the single instrument that has done most to change what a farmer may legally do with a harvest, and it spreads through trade negotiation rather than through domestic debate. Most people affected by it have never heard of it.

name: Codex Alimentarius — foods derived from biotechnology
desc: WHAT. The joint FAO/WHO food standards body, whose guidelines on the safety assessment of foods derived from modern biotechnology are the international reference. WHERE IT SITS. The standard that WTO dispute panels look to when a country's restriction is challenged as a trade barrier. WHY IT MATTERS. A voluntary guideline becomes effectively binding once trade law treats departure from it as an obstacle needing justification. This is the mechanism by which an advisory standard constrains national decisions, and it is how the Mexico ruling worked.

name: European Food Safety Authority — GMO panel opinions
desc: WHAT. The scientific opinions underpinning every EU authorisation, published in full with the panel's reasoning, the data considered and the minority positions where they exist. WHERE IT SITS. The assessment step between an application and a Commission decision, for the world's largest import market. WHY IT MATTERS. The opinions run to hundreds of pages and are open for public comment for thirty days after publication. Almost nobody comments. It is the most consequential open door on this map and the one least walked through.

name: Vietnam — GM maize cultivation and feed imports
desc: WHAT. Vietnam's agriculture ministry, which authorised GM maize cultivation and oversees very large feed-grain imports for the livestock sector. WHERE IT SITS. One of the few Southeast Asian countries growing engineered crops as well as importing them. WHY IT MATTERS. Vietnam's livestock expansion drives the feed demand, and the feed demand drives the imports and the domestic cultivation together. The trait decision follows the animal-production decision, which is the sequence almost everywhere and almost never how the argument is framed.

name: Institute for Agricultural Research, Zaria — Bt cowpea
desc: WHAT. The Nigerian public institute that developed and released Bt cowpea, the first engineered food crop grown commercially in sub-Saharan Africa outside South Africa. WHERE IT SITS. A public breeding programme deploying a donated corporate trait with foreign development funding. WHY IT MATTERS. Cowpea is a staple grown and eaten locally rather than exported, so this is one of very few engineered crops aimed at the people who grow it. It is also the model the industry now prefers in low-income countries: the trait is donated, the public institute carries the approval and the reputation, and the company carries neither the cost nor the blame.

name: Egypt — wheat import tenders and GM specification
desc: WHAT. Egypt's state grain buyer, which runs the world's largest wheat import tenders and sets the specifications suppliers must meet. WHERE IT SITS. The single largest buyer of wheat on Earth, writing purchase conditions that exporters reorganise around. WHY IT MATTERS. Tender specifications are commercial documents that function as regulation. What the largest buyer accepts becomes what exporters supply, and that decision is made by a purchasing agency rather than by any biosafety authority.

name: Pivot Bio — PROVEN product record
desc: WHAT. The company's product material for its engineered nitrogen-fixing microbes, applied to maize, wheat and other cereals across millions of US acres. WHERE IT SITS. The largest commercial deployment of an engineered microbe onto farmland anywhere. WHY IT MATTERS. Applied at that acreage it is one of the largest deliberate releases of an engineered organism in history by area, and it generates no entry in any biosafety register because a soil microbe applied to seed is not a plant and is not planted. The scale and the invisibility are both facts about the same product.

name: Marrone / Pro Farm Group
desc: WHAT. A biopesticide company producing microbial and plant-derived crop protection products, now part of a larger consolidated biologicals business. WHERE IT SITS. The mid-tier of agricultural biologicals, in a sector consolidating fast into the same four majors. WHY IT MATTERS. Biologicals are following the seed sector's trajectory a generation later. The pattern is visible early enough to name now rather than after it completes, which is rarely possible.

name: USDA APHIS — biotechnology regulatory notices
desc: WHAT. The public notices of new permit applications, deregulation petitions and requests for comment on engineered organisms in the United States. WHERE IT SITS. The comment window — the only point at which an outsider's objection formally enters the file. WHY IT MATTERS. Comment periods are short, published in one place, and generate no notification unless you subscribe. The window is real and it closes quietly, which is why almost every consequential decision on this map passed with a handful of comments or none.

name: ViaGen — Przewalski's horse and endangered species cloning
desc: WHAT. The commercial cloning company that produced cloned Przewalski's horses from cryopreserved cells, working with San Diego Zoo and Revive & Restore. WHERE IT SITS. The same company that clones pets for paying customers, doing conservation work with the same technology. WHY IT MATTERS. Commercial pet cloning built the capability that conservation cloning now uses. Whatever one thinks of either, the capacity exists because a consumer market paid to develop it, and that is worth knowing before treating the two as separate industries.

name: Wildlife Conservation Society — biotechnology position
desc: WHAT. One of the largest conservation organisations, which manages field programmes worldwide and holds a position in the sector's debate over engineered organisms in conservation. WHERE IT SITS. Among the bodies whose eventual stance will decide whether engineered releases become a normal conservation tool. WHY IT MATTERS. Large conservation organisations hold land, credibility and regulator access. Which way they go on this will matter more than most national positions, and the internal argument is happening now with very little outside attention.

name: Vertex Pharmaceuticals
desc: WHAT. The company that commercialised Casgevy with CRISPR Therapeutics, and whose cystic fibrosis franchise is among the most profitable in medicine. WHERE IT SITS. The commercial partner that takes an editing platform through approval, manufacture and pricing. WHY IT MATTERS. The scientific credit for CRISPR sits with the academic founders; the pricing decision sits here. Separating those two is how the field discusses itself, and holding them together is the point of putting both on one map.

name: National Marrow Donor Program / NMDP — cell therapy infrastructure
desc: WHAT. The registry and infrastructure for stem cell transplantation in the United States, which the delivery of ex-vivo gene therapies depends on. WHERE IT SITS. The clinical infrastructure a gene therapy needs to be given at all — transplant-grade facilities, conditioning regimens, matched care. WHY IT MATTERS. A therapy requiring this infrastructure cannot reach anywhere that lacks it, regardless of price. For the sickle cell therapies that means most of the population with the disease, and the barrier is hospitals rather than money.

name: Sickle Cell Disease Association of America
desc: WHAT. The patient organisation representing people with sickle cell disease in the United States, active on access to the new gene therapies. WHERE IT SITS. The constituency for the first approved CRISPR therapy, and the one least represented in how it was priced. WHY IT MATTERS. Patient organisations are frequently funded in part by the companies whose products they advocate for, which is disclosed and is worth knowing. It also remains the case that the people affected have the least say in the decisions that determine whether a cure reaches them.

name: Fidelity and index funds — passive ownership of the sector
desc: WHAT. The SEC filings showing that large index and asset managers are among the biggest shareholders of nearly every listed company on this map. WHERE IT SITS. The ownership layer above the named companies, which nobody chose company by company. WHY IT MATTERS. Index funds own these companies because they own the index. That makes most people with a pension part-owners of this industry, and it is the mechanism that makes shareholder pressure possible at all — the same fact cuts both ways and this map should say so.

name: Bill & Melinda Gates Agricultural Innovations (Gates Ag One)
desc: WHAT. A non-profit subsidiary of the Gates Foundation created to accelerate agricultural research toward smallholder farmers in Africa and South Asia, holding and licensing intellectual property. WHERE IT SITS. Philanthropic capital operating as a technology transfer organisation rather than a grantmaker. WHY IT MATTERS. It holds IP with the stated aim of licensing it royalty-free to smallholders. That is a different model from either corporate ownership or public domain, and whether it delivers differently is testable rather than assumed — the licences are the place to check.

name: Rothamsted — GM aphid-repellent wheat trial
desc: WHAT. The public record of the engineered wheat trial designed to repel aphids, including the published result that it did not work in the field. WHERE IT SITS. A publicly funded trial that reported a negative result in full. WHY IT MATTERS. The trait worked in the glasshouse and failed in the field, and the institute published that. Negative results from developers are rare enough on this map to mark wherever they appear — and this one is the single best answer to the claim that laboratory performance predicts field performance.

name: CSIRO — agricultural biotechnology
desc: WHAT. Australia's national science agency, which developed engineered safflower for industrial oils, omega-3 canola with Nuseed, and holds substantial crop biotechnology patents. WHERE IT SITS. Public research that licenses its traits commercially, in the country with the most detailed release register in the world. WHY IT MATTERS. CSIRO's traits appear in the OGTR record with their licences and conditions attached, which makes it possible to follow a publicly funded trait from laboratory to commercial licence in a way that is impossible almost anywhere else.

name: Rhino and wildlife biobanking — BioRescue partners
desc: WHAT. The consortium attempting to produce northern white rhino embryos from cryopreserved cells and harvested oocytes, with only two living females of the subspecies remaining. WHERE IT SITS. The most advanced attempt anywhere to bring a functionally extinct large mammal back through assisted reproduction. WHY IT MATTERS. It is the clearest case of biotechnology deployed after every other option failed, on a subspecies driven to two individuals by poaching. Whatever it demonstrates about the technology, it demonstrates more about what made it necessary.

name: PMDA — regenerative medicine conditional approval
desc: WHAT. Japan's regulator, which operates a conditional and time-limited approval pathway for regenerative medicine products, allowing marketing on preliminary evidence. WHERE IT SITS. The most permissive major approval route for cell and gene therapies in the world. WHY IT MATTERS. Products have been marketed in Japan on evidence that would not support approval elsewhere, and at least one was later withdrawn when confirmatory data did not arrive. It is the working experiment in whether early access or evidence should come first, and the results are being generated on patients.

name: Chinese state agricultural investment — seed industry revitalisation
desc: WHAT. China's agriculture ministry, running the national seed industry programme that has directed very large state investment into domestic breeding and biotechnology since 2021. WHERE IT SITS. State capital rebuilding a national seed sector explicitly to reduce dependence on foreign traits. WHY IT MATTERS. Seed sovereignty is being pursued as industrial policy by the world's largest agricultural producer, with the state as investor, regulator and customer. It is the clearest case anywhere of a government treating seed as strategic infrastructure rather than as a market.

name: Aurigene / Dr Reddy's discovery services
desc: WHAT. The discovery and development services arm of a large Indian pharmaceutical group, running biology and chemistry programmes for international clients. WHERE IT SITS. The discovery end of the contract layer, in the country taking a growing share of it. WHY IT MATTERS. Discovery outsourcing means the earliest decisions about what gets pursued are made inside contractors, shaped by what is tractable and fundable. Those decisions precede every regulator by years and are recorded nowhere public.

name: SK pharmteco
desc: WHAT. A contract manufacturer of small molecules and cell and gene therapies, part of the SK group, with sites in Korea, the United States and France. WHERE IT SITS. Asian-owned manufacturing capacity inside Western jurisdictions, serving Western clients. WHY IT MATTERS. Policy arguments about reducing dependence on Asian manufacturing routinely conflate ownership with location. A plant in France owned by a Korean group is subject to French regulation and Korean corporate decisions, and only one of those is what the policy is aimed at.

name: Ministry of Agriculture — GMO cultivation prohibition
desc: WHAT. Poland's agriculture ministry, administering a prohibition on the cultivation of GM crops enacted through seed law rather than biosafety law. WHERE IT SITS. One of the EU member states using seed marketing rules to achieve what a cultivation ban would. WHY IT MATTERS. Prohibiting the marketing of GM seed achieves a cultivation ban without invoking the biosafety framework at all. It is a route several countries have used, and it works because seed law is where the practical control sits.

name: Malaysian Palm Oil Board — genome programme
desc: WHAT. The state palm oil authority, which sequenced the oil palm genome and runs breeding and editing research on yield and disease resistance. WHERE IT SITS. A state body holding the genomic resources of a crop that is both a major export earner and a target for replacement by fermented substitutes. WHY IT MATTERS. Malaysia is being offered the upgrade and the replacement at once — engineered palm improvement on one side, precision-fermented oils designed to displace palm oil on the other. A producing country in that position has no obvious side to take, and the usual framing does not cover it.

name: S&W Seed Company
desc: WHAT. A breeder and marketer of alfalfa, sorghum and forage seed, including herbicide-tolerant alfalfa varieties. WHERE IT SITS. Forage crops, which are perennial, insect-pollinated and grown next to everything else. WHY IT MATTERS. Alfalfa is pollinated by bees that forage far beyond any buffer distance, and stands persist for years. It is the crop where coexistence rules written around annual, self-pollinating plants fit worst, and it was approved for release anyway.

name: Simplot — Innate potatoes
desc: WHAT. Engineered potatoes with reduced bruising, lower acrylamide and blight resistance, developed using potato genes rather than foreign ones. WHERE IT SITS. Cisgenics — engineering using genes from the same species or a sexually compatible one. WHY IT MATTERS. The traits are consumer-facing rather than farmer-facing, which is what the industry is repeatedly asked to produce. It is also a whole-food product sold unlabelled in most markets, so a consumer choosing on the basis of the improvement cannot verify it either way.

name: J.R. Simplot / McCain — processor specification
desc: WHAT. The largest potato processors in the world, whose contracts specify the varieties growers may plant. WHERE IT SITS. Between the breeder and the field, deciding what actually gets grown. WHY IT MATTERS. Processor specification is why the engineered potato has had a limited market: the buyers declined it, and growers plant what buyers will take. It is the market door working, documented, in a crop where it was decisive.

name: Perfect Day
desc: WHAT. A company producing dairy proteins by fermentation using engineered fungi, sold as ingredients in ice cream, milk alternatives and protein products. WHERE IT SITS. Precision fermentation — an animal product made without the animal, from an engineered organism that never reaches the consumer. WHY IT MATTERS. The protein is identical to the dairy version and the engineered organism is removed during processing, so in most jurisdictions nothing requires a label. It is one of the largest routes by which engineered-organism products reach households, and the least visible.

name: Impossible Foods — soy leghemoglobin
desc: WHAT. A plant-based meat company whose defining ingredient is a heme protein produced by engineered yeast, approved as a colour additive in the United States. WHERE IT SITS. The most prominent consumer product on this map that depends on an engineered organism and says so. WHY IT MATTERS. It is unusual in this facet for being open about it, and the disclosure has cost it with part of its own natural-foods constituency. That tension — a product marketed on environmental grounds and opposed on genetic ones — is one the map should show rather than resolve.

name: Conagen
desc: WHAT. A company producing flavours, sweeteners, vitamins and cosmetic ingredients by fermentation with engineered microorganisms. WHERE IT SITS. Ingredient substitution — compounds previously extracted from plants, now brewed. WHY IT MATTERS. Fermented substitutes displace agricultural livelihoods without appearing in any agricultural policy debate. When a compound harvested in one country starts being made in a tank in another, the growers have no forum in which to raise it.

name: Charles River — horseshoe crab and LAL supply
desc: WHAT. The endotoxin testing reagent made from horseshoe crab blood, used to test injectable drugs and devices for bacterial contamination, alongside the recombinant synthetic alternative. WHERE IT SITS. A wild animal harvested at scale for a reagent every injectable medicine depends on. WHY IT MATTERS. A recombinant replacement exists, works and has been accepted into the US pharmacopoeia, and adoption has been slow because the established test is what regulators and manufacturers are used to. **Here the engineered substitute is the option that spares the animals, and inertia is what keeps it from being used.**

name: Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees — OLAW
desc: WHAT. The NIH office overseeing the committees that approve animal research protocols at every institution receiving federal funds. WHERE IT SITS. The approval layer inside each institution, staffed by that institution. WHY IT MATTERS. Protocol review is done by colleagues of the researcher, at the institution whose funding depends on the research proceeding. Committee minutes are frequently obtainable at public universities under freedom of information law, and almost nobody requests them.

name: Editas Medicine
desc: WHAT. A CRISPR company that ran the first in-vivo gene editing trial in humans, injecting an editor directly into the eye to treat an inherited blindness, and later discontinued the programme. WHERE IT SITS. The first attempt to edit inside a living person, and the first to be stopped for commercial rather than safety reasons. WHY IT MATTERS. The trial showed the approach could work in some patients and the company ended it because the market was too small. Participants accepted an irreversible procedure in a programme that was then discontinued, which is a risk of trial participation nobody consents to explicitly.

name: Orchard Therapeutics
desc: WHAT. A gene therapy company focused on rare inherited disorders, whose approved therapies include treatment for metachromatic leukodystrophy. WHERE IT SITS. Ultra-rare disease, where the eligible population is a few hundred children worldwide. WHY IT MATTERS. Therapies for populations this small cannot recover development cost at any plausible volume, so the price per patient becomes extraordinary by arithmetic rather than by choice. It is the honest version of the pricing argument, and it does not apply to the larger indications where the same prices are charged.

name: Euralis / Lidea
desc: WHAT. A large European field seed company formed from cooperative breeding businesses, selling maize, sunflower, soy and rapeseed varieties across Europe and beyond. WHERE IT SITS. Cooperative-rooted breeding, competing with the majors in a market where GM cultivation is largely closed. WHY IT MATTERS. European field breeding continued and consolidated without GM traits, which is the working answer to the claim that a market cannot function without them. Whether the varieties perform as well is a real question; that the sector exists is not.

name: TMG — Tropical Melhoramento & Genética
desc: WHAT. A Brazilian soy and cotton breeder that licenses traits from the majors and develops varieties adapted to tropical conditions. WHERE IT SITS. The adaptation layer — a trait is useless without a variety bred for the local climate and disease pressure. WHY IT MATTERS. Traits travel; varieties do not. The majors' traits reach Brazilian fields only because local breeders put them into locally adapted germplasm, which makes those breeders a chokepoint nobody counts when measuring concentration.

name: European Sperm Bank
desc: WHAT. One of Europe's largest gamete banks, exporting donor sperm internationally with published donor profiles and family limits. WHERE IT SITS. Alongside Cryos in a Danish sector that supplies much of Europe and beyond. WHY IT MATTERS. Denmark's rules permit export at a scale the importing countries' own family limits were never written to contemplate. Two banks in one small country substantially determine how many half-siblings a donor-conceived person in another country may have.

name: Greek cross-border fertility sector
desc: WHAT. Greece's health ministry, regulating a fertility sector that has become a major destination for cross-border treatment, including egg donation and surrogacy. WHERE IT SITS. One of the small number of European jurisdictions whose rules attract patients from countries with stricter ones. WHY IT MATTERS. Cross-border reproductive care is regulated by the destination and paid for by the visitor, so the country writing the rules bears none of the consequences of them. That mismatch is the structural feature of this whole market.

name: WTO — SPS Committee and biotechnology notifications
desc: WHAT. The committee where members notify and challenge each other's sanitary and phytosanitary measures, including approval delays and GM restrictions. WHERE IT SITS. Where a country's biosafety decision becomes a trade complaint. WHY IT MATTERS. Members raise 'specific trade concerns' about each other's biotechnology approval timelines, and the record of those exchanges is public. It is the clearest documentation anywhere of pressure applied to regulators from outside their own country.

name: ISO — biotechnology standards committee
desc: WHAT. The international standards committee developing technical standards for biotechnology, including biobanking, biological resources and analytical methods. WHERE IT SITS. Below regulation and above practice — the technical definitions everything else is written on top of. WHY IT MATTERS. Standards committees are open to participation and almost nobody outside industry participates. A definition settled here propagates into national regulation years later without anyone having argued about it in public.

name: COMESA — regional biosafety policy
desc: WHAT. The Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa's regional guidelines on commercial planting, trade and emergency food aid involving GM material. WHERE IT SITS. Regional harmonisation covering twenty-one member states. WHY IT MATTERS. Regional guidelines move many countries at once without each holding a separate national debate, which is efficient and is also how a position spreads faster than opposition to it can organise. The same mechanism as the African Union model law, at a different scale.

name: Volcani Center — Agricultural Research Organization
desc: WHAT. Israel's national agricultural research institute, running crop genetics, editing and desert-agriculture programmes and licensing varieties internationally. WHERE IT SITS. Public agricultural research in a country that exports agricultural technology far more than agricultural produce. WHY IT MATTERS. Israel's agricultural exports are largely knowledge and inputs rather than food, which makes its research priorities respond to what other countries will buy rather than to what it grows. That is an unusual and under-examined driver of what gets developed.

name: International Center for Biosaline Agriculture
desc: WHAT. A research centre in Dubai working on crops for saline soils and water-scarce environments, including quinoa and salt-tolerant forages. WHERE IT SITS. The environments conventional breeding has served worst, and where drought and salinity tolerance would matter most. WHY IT MATTERS. The traits this map notes as absent from commercial pipelines — poor-soil yield, salinity and drought tolerance — are being worked on here, largely by conventional breeding and largely on public and philanthropic money. That is where they are, and it is a fraction of the resources going into the two commercial traits.

name: International Potato Center (CIP)
desc: WHAT. The CGIAR centre holding the world's largest potato and sweetpotato genebank, in the crop's centre of origin, running breeding and biofortification programmes. WHERE IT SITS. Inside a national GMO moratorium, holding the global genetic reservoir for a staple crop. WHY IT MATTERS. A centre of origin, a genebank and a national moratorium in one place is the configuration the Cartagena Protocol's centre-of-origin provisions were written for. It is also where the biofortified sweetpotato work happened — conventional breeding delivering the nutrition trait the engineered pipeline is criticised for not delivering.

name: Ethiopian Biodiversity Institute
desc: WHAT. The national genebank and biodiversity authority, holding one of Africa's oldest and largest collections of crop landraces and wild relatives. WHERE IT SITS. A centre of origin for coffee, sorghum, teff and enset, with the collection to match. WHY IT MATTERS. It was among the first institutions anywhere to insist on material transfer terms and benefit sharing for its collections, decades before the Nagoya Protocol. The precedent came from a low-income country protecting its own material, not from an international negotiation.

name: Corteva — hybrid wheat programme
desc: WHAT. The commercial hybrid wheat programme, which would replace self-pollinating open varieties with hybrids a farmer cannot usefully save. WHERE IT SITS. Wheat, the crop the industry has repeatedly failed to enter and keeps returning to. WHY IT MATTERS. Hybridisation achieves what a patent achieves without needing one: the saved seed simply does not perform. It is the oldest mechanism in this whole map for making a farmer buy every year, and it requires no law at all.

name: Bayer — short-stature corn
desc: WHAT. Maize bred and edited to grow roughly a third shorter, marketed as more resistant to lodging in high winds. WHERE IT SITS. A trait responding to weather rather than to weeds or pests — the first of the two commercial categories to be joined by a third. WHY IT MATTERS. Short-stature corn is an adaptation to a climate producing stronger storms. The industry is now selling adaptation to conditions its own input-intensive model contributes to, which is a closed loop worth naming plainly.

name: Corteva — Enlist herbicide system
desc: WHAT. The 2,4-D-tolerant trait and matched herbicide system, developed as glyphosate resistance spread through weed populations. WHERE IT SITS. The second generation of the seed-and-spray pair, sold because the first one stopped working. WHY IT MATTERS. It is the treadmill made visible in a product line: resistance to one chemical is answered with tolerance to another, and the older herbicides now being reintroduced drift further and damage neighbouring crops more than the one they replace.

name: Ohalo Genetics
desc: WHAT. A company developing 'boosted breeding', a technique intended to pass both parents' full genomes to offspring rather than half of each. WHERE IT SITS. A change to the mechanics of inheritance itself rather than to any particular gene. WHY IT MATTERS. Every regulatory category on this map is built around what was inserted or edited. A technique that alters how genomes combine, without adding or changing a sequence, does not obviously fall inside any of them — and the frameworks would have to be rewritten to reach it.

name: Syngenta — biologicals and Valagro
desc: WHAT. The company's biologicals business, built substantially through the acquisition of the Italian biostimulant firm Valagro. WHERE IT SITS. A major moving into biologicals by purchase rather than by development. WHY IT MATTERS. This is the consolidation of the biologicals sector happening in real time: the independents this map listed a few rounds ago are the acquisition targets, and the same four names are assembling the next input category as they assembled the last one.

name: BASF — enzymes and industrial biotechnology
desc: WHAT. BASF's enzyme, vitamin and feed-additive businesses, produced by fermentation with engineered microorganisms. WHERE IT SITS. The same company that sells seed and crop protection also makes engineered-organism products for feed and food processing. WHY IT MATTERS. The four majors are usually discussed as seed and pesticide companies. Their fermentation businesses put engineered organisms into the food system by an entirely different route, unlabelled, and are almost never counted when their reach is measured.

name: dsm-firmenich
desc: WHAT. A very large nutrition, health and flavours company producing vitamins, enzymes, feed additives and the methane-reducing feed supplement Bovaer, much of it by fermentation. WHERE IT SITS. Between the engineered microbe and the supermarket, in products nobody associates with biotechnology. WHY IT MATTERS. Its feed additive became the subject of a large consumer backlash despite not being an engineered organism in the final product, which showed how little of this argument tracks what is actually in the food. The company's genuinely engineered products drew none of that attention.

name: Novo Nordisk — recombinant insulin manufacture
desc: WHAT. One of the two dominant insulin producers, making recombinant human insulin and analogues with engineered yeast and bacteria at very large scale. WHERE IT SITS. The oldest commercial product of genetic engineering, made by three companies for most of the world. WHY IT MATTERS. Recombinant insulin is the field's founding success and its clearest pricing scandal at once: the technique is fifty years old, the patents long expired, and the price in some markets rose anyway because three firms supply nearly all of it. **Age and expired patents do not produce low prices; competition does, and here there is little.**

name: Biocon — biosimilar insulin
desc: WHAT. An Indian company producing recombinant insulin and biosimilars at prices far below the originators', supplying low- and middle-income markets. WHERE IT SITS. The competitive answer to the insulin concentration named above. WHY IT MATTERS. It demonstrates that the price of a recombinant medicine can fall a long way when someone else makes it, which locates the cause of high prices in market structure rather than in manufacturing difficulty. That distinction is checkable, and this is where to check it.

name: Oxford Nanopore — field sequencing
desc: WHAT. Handheld sequencers used for pathogen surveillance, food authentication and biodiversity work outside a laboratory. WHERE IT SITS. Sequencing taken out of the building — including to a field, a border post or a river. WHY IT MATTERS. Portable sequencing is the one technology on this map that materially helps the people checking rather than the people releasing. Verifying what is in a seed lot, a shipment or a wild population becomes possible without an institutional laboratory, and that is a genuine shift in who can find things out.

name: Roslin Institute
desc: WHAT. The institute that produced Dolly the sheep and now runs livestock gene-editing programmes including disease-resistant pigs and poultry. WHERE IT SITS. The origin of animal cloning and a continuing centre of farm animal engineering. WHY IT MATTERS. Dolly is where public argument about animal biotechnology began, and the institute has been working continuously since. Reading its current programme alongside the 1996 coverage shows how completely the argument moved on while the work carried straight through it.

name: Yuan Longping High-Tech Agriculture
desc: WHAT. A large Chinese seed company named for the hybrid rice breeder, working across rice, maize and now GM traits. WHERE IT SITS. A national champion in the crop that feeds most of Asia.
